verdict: OK to lend in Vadodara engineering & capital goods — pursue export-linked, order-book-backed OEMs and fabricators; avoid EPC-heavy and thin-margin casting units until receivables and margin data are verified.
title: Vadodara Engineering & Capital Goods: a note to the credit manager
narrative: Value sits in the order book and the customer relationship, not the machine. Cash sits in receivables and work-in-progress, so **the working-capital cycle is the credit, not the plant** [9][11]. Pricing power is thin where the product is a commodity fabrication; it is real where the unit is a qualified vendor to a marquee OEM.

## What has changed now
**The demand signal is genuinely strong: IIP for NIC 28 (machinery) is up 10.3% YoY and 10.4% Apr-to-date, and exports are up 19.8% Apr-to-date in USD** [D]. Gujarat GST collections are running +11.9% Apr-to-date against India's +6.1% [D], so the local order flow is real. But peer results show the split clearly: DEE's revenue rose 77% YoY to ₹286.7 crore with operating profit at ₹47.6 crore [5], and Skipper posted its highest-ever Q2 revenue with PAT up 56% [6] — while Suzlon grew revenue 26% to ₹4,869 crore but EBITDA stayed flat at ₹720 crore and margin fell to 14.8% from 18.6% [7]. **Volume is not margin.** Pitti is expanding a Hyderabad casting facility through FY2030 on data-centre, mining and railway order visibility [4] — good for them, but it tells you capex is being committed against order books that must actually execute.

## Where the growth is — who to pursue
**Pursue the export-linked fabricator and the qualified-vendor OEM supplier.** Exports at +19.8% Apr-to-date [D] and the FGI EXIM Conclave in Vadodara [3] point to units with real overseas buyers. Pursue piping and fittings makers serving oil & gas, given DEE's execution rebound [5], and T&D structure makers given Skipper's record order book [6]. **Avoid the pure EPC contractor and the single-customer casting shop** until you see the cash conversion cycle — CRISIL notes EPC cash cycles run higher than OEMs because of longer execution periods [11].

## How to grow safely
**Structure every limit against the order book, not the balance sheet.** Take assignment of receivables or a charge on the order book where the buyer is a marquee name. Set the drawing power on verified receivables ageing, not on stock. **Take every month: stock-and-receivable statement, ageing bucket beyond 90 days, order-book position with buyer names, and GST returns matched to sales.** If the receivable days exceed the sanction assumption, ask for the buyer-wise ageing and the contract payment terms before renewing. Where the unit is bidding for orders, note that performance bank guarantees consume limit — size the non-fund-based line separately [9].

## Early-warning signs
**Watch margin before you watch revenue.** If EBITDA margin slips the way Suzlon's did — 14.8% from 18.6% [7] — while sales grow, the unit is buying volume. Watch receivable days stretching past the contract terms, inventory building against a stalled order, and any capex announced without named buyers. Vadodara-specific coverage in our sources is thin — the local items are an exhibition notice [1] and a conclave post [3], and one local source is a demo page [2] — so lean on first principles and the peer set above. Collect from customer: city-level order-book data, unit-wise receivable days, and buyer concentration.
watch: 90+ day bucket crosses 25% of book -> freeze enhancement, ask for buyer-wise ageing
Margin falls while revenue grows -> reprice or reduce limit
Order book falls below 6 months of revenue -> shift to receivables-backed structure
Gap above 10% between GST turnover and invoiced sales -> stop disbursement, verify
Non-fund limit above 80% utilised -> resize line before new bid
watch_note: Trigger levels are policy suggestions (analytical framing), not data.
